summary: Teach formal columnar addition and subtraction to three digits as a compact written algorithm that keeps its place-value meaning. Introduce it only after children can compose/decompose concretely, and bridge from the expanded method (partial sums) to the compact one so each carried or exchanged digit still stands for a real ten or hundred. The skill has three parts: correct place-value alignment, the carry/exchange mechanic, and checking with estimation or the inverse. Pair written work with place-value counters during the transition, and rehearse the hard across-zero exchange explicitly.
misconceptions: Place-value misalignment: writing digits ragged so ones and tens are added together
Smaller-from-larger: subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column regardless of position (83−25→62 pattern, now at three digits)
Carry omitted or mis-placed: forgetting to add the carried ten/hundred to the next column
Borrow-across-zero errors when the adjacent column is 0 (502−276)

activities.title: Carry and exchange with counters beside the columns
steps: Set out 347 + 185 in columns on squared paper or a headed H-T-O grid, ones under ones.

Add the ones: 7 + 5 = 12. Write the 2 in the ones column and the carried 1 above the tens; alongside, exchange ten of the 12 one-counters for a single ten-counter and place it in the tens column, so the written '1' and the real ten move together.
Add the tens: 4 + 8 + 1 = 13. Write 3, carry 1 hundred, and exchange ten of the 13 ten-counters for a single hundred-counter, placing it in the hundreds column.

Now set out 502 − 276. To take 6 from 2 in the ones you need more ones, but the tens column is 0: first break one hundred into ten tens (502 becomes 400 + 90 + 12 after the cascade), then break a ten into ten ones.
Estimate first by rounding (≈ 350 + 200 = 550, or 300 + 200 = 500, for the addition; ≈ 500 − 280 = 220 for the subtraction) and check the subtraction by adding 226 + 276 back to 502.
activities.insight: A carried or exchanged digit is a real ten or hundred moving between columns, not a meaningless mark; across a zero you must decompose a hundred into tens before you can get a ten, then a ten into ones.

activities.title: Bridge from expanded partial sums to the compact column
steps: Solve 347 + 185 first in the expanded written layout, writing each partial sum: 7 + 5 = 12, 40 + 80 = 120, 300 + 100 = 400.
Add the partial sums (12 + 120 + 400 = 532) and notice where the extra ten and the extra hundred come from.
Rewrite the same calculation in the compact column, carrying the 1 ten and 1 hundred, and check the answer matches 532.
Say aloud what each carried digit in the compact version stands for, pointing back to the partial sum it came from.
activities.insight: The compact algorithm is a shorthand for the expanded method; every carry corresponds to a partial sum crossing into the next place.

activities.title: Spot the error in a worked column
steps: Examine a worked example where the digits are set out ragged (for example the 5 of 185 placed under the 4 of 347) and identify what has gone wrong and why the answer is unreliable.
Examine a worked across-zero subtraction where a 9 or 0 has been written at the empty tens column without decomposing a hundred, and explain the correct cascade.
Rework each flawed example correctly on a headed grid and state what the fixed carry or exchange represents.
Complete a few mixed column calculations for fluency, estimating first and checking with the inverse.
activities.insight: Many errors that look careless are the surface of a systematic wrong procedure (misalignment, smaller-from-larger, borrow-across-zero); naming the bug helps avoid it.

activities.title: Explain your steps aloud
steps: After solving a column calculation, answer: 'Point to the little 1 you carried — what does that 1 actually stand for?'
For 502 − 276, explain: 'There were no tens to take from — how did you get them?'
Justify the estimate: 'Round 347 + 185 — is your answer sensible?'
Verify: 'Add your subtraction answer to 276 — does it come back to 502?'
activities.insight: Articulating why a carry or exchange happens exposes whether the procedure is understood or merely copied.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to set out and solve two calculations in columns on squared paper, then check each: 347 + 185, then 502 − 276. Watch how they align the digits, handle the carry, and manage the exchange across the zero.
checkAnswer: 532 and 226. 347+185: ones 7+5=12 (write 2, carry 1 ten), tens 4+8+1=13 (write 3, carry 1 hundred), hundreds 3+1+1=5 → 532. 502−276: exchange needed in ones but tens is 0, so decompose a hundred to tens then a ten to ones (502 as 400+90+12), 12−6=6, 90−70=20, 400−200=200 → 226.
